recent_posts.title: A Social Filesystem — overreacted
recent_posts.summary: The AT Protocol reimagines social media using a filesystem paradigm where user data lives in personal repositories as JSON records, not trapped inside apps. Each user has an 'everything folder' containing collections of records (posts, likes, follows) defined by lexicons—schemas that work like file formats. Apps become reactive views over this distributed social filesystem. Identity uses DIDs (decentralized identifiers) that survive hosting changes, enabling permanent at:// links to records. Records reference each other across users' repositories, forming a web of JSON. Apps subscribe to repository streams, cache relevant slices, and compute derived data locally. This separation means users control their data, can switch hosting providers, and multiple apps can operate on the same underlying records—making third-party experiences first-class citizens.

recent_posts.title: Introducing RSC Explorer — overreacted
recent_posts.summary: RSC Explorer is a new browser-based tool that visualizes how React Server Components (RSC) protocol works. It demonstrates how React serializes and deserializes component trees over the network, showing streaming behavior, client-server code references, Server Actions, and routing patterns. The tool runs entirely client-side using React's actual RSC packages, allowing developers to step through examples and understand the protocol's implementation details without needing a framework.

recent_posts.title: Dan Abramov seeks software engineering role in Japan with visa sponsorship
recent_posts.summary: Dan Abramov, known for his work on React at Meta and the Bluesky app, is seeking a software engineering position in Japan with visa sponsorship. He recaps his 15+ years of professional experience, including creating React Hooks documentation, Fast Refresh, Create React App, and Redux. He's looking for roles in UI engineering and web development, preferably in Kyoto, with English as the primary work language while he learns Japanese.

recent_posts.title: A systematic approach to debugging any software bug
recent_posts.summary: A systematic approach to debugging is presented through a real-world example of fixing a scroll jitter bug in a React Router application. The methodology emphasizes creating reliable reproduction cases, narrowing them down incrementally, and maintaining discipline by only committing changes that preserve the bug. The process involves trading complex repros for simpler ones, ensuring each simplified version still captures the original issue, and systematically removing code until the root cause emerges. The bug turned out to be an outdated React Router version where ScrollRestoration triggered on revalidation instead of route changes.

recent_posts.title: How to resolve AT protocol URIs step by step
recent_posts.summary: A technical deep dive into how AT protocol URIs work, explaining the three-step resolution process: converting handles to decentralized identifiers (DIDs), locating hosting servers through DID Documents, and retrieving JSON data. The post walks through practical examples of resolving at:// URIs, comparing did:web and did:plc identity methods, and demonstrates how the protocol separates user identity from data hosting to enable portability.

recent_posts.title: How open social protocols could transform social media like open source transformed software
recent_posts.summary: Explores the concept of "open social" through the AT Protocol, drawing parallels between how open source transformed software development and how decentralized social networks could transform social media. The protocol enables users to own their social data in personal repositories while still enabling aggregation features like feeds and notifications. Users can migrate between platforms without losing their social graph, and applications can interoperate by sharing data formats. This approach aims to solve the vendor lock-in problem of current social media platforms where user data becomes trapped in proprietary databases.

recent_posts.title: Lean for JavaScript Developers — overreacted
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive syntax primer for the Lean programming language, written specifically for JavaScript developers. Covers fundamental concepts including definitions, types, functions, proofs, and the unique ability to write programs alongside mathematical proofs. Demonstrates how Lean combines traditional programming with formal verification, allowing developers to prove properties about their code during compilation.

recent_posts.title: Beyond Booleans — overreacted
recent_posts.summary: Explores how Lean handles logical propositions differently from traditional programming languages like TypeScript. Instead of collapsing logical expressions into boolean values, Lean treats propositions as distinct types that require proofs to establish their truth. The article demonstrates the Curry-Howard correspondence, showing how mathematical proofs can be expressed as values of proposition types, enabling typed truthfulness where facts can be verified at compile time and composed into more complex logical arguments.

recent_posts.title: Introduction to Lean programming language for mathematical proofs
recent_posts.summary: Lean is a programming language designed for formalizing mathematics, allowing mathematicians to treat mathematical proofs as code. The article demonstrates basic Lean concepts through simple examples, showing how theorems are proven using tactics like 'rfl' and 'exact', and how axioms can lead to contradictions. It explores the relationship between axioms and mathematical soundness, using examples from proving '2 = 2' to the ongoing formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean.
